semantic_correction.stem: A parent asks why an immunocompetent 11-year-old who has never received HPV vaccine should start the series now. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: Start HPV vaccination now; at age 11 it is routine, and an immunocompetent child starting before age 15 receives 2 doses 6–12 months apart to prevent new HPV infection.
options.B: Delay HPV vaccination until adulthood, when prior HPV exposure can be confirmed; vaccination works best after exposure and an 11-year-old does not yet need routine protection.
options.C: Wait to vaccinate until an HPV infection or related lesion is identified, because the vaccine is used to treat existing HPV disease rather than prevent future infection.
options.D: Offer HPV vaccination to girls at age 11 but not routinely to boys, because the cancers prevented by HPV vaccination occur primarily in the female reproductive tract.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. The current CDC child/adolescent schedule recommends routine HPV vaccination at age 11–12 years and permits starting at age 9. For an immunocompetent person who begins the series at ages 9–14 years, the routine schedule is 2 doses at 0 and 6–12 months. CDC also states that HPV vaccination prevents new HPV infections, does not treat existing infection or disease, and works best before HPV exposure. B is incorrect because delaying until adulthood forfeits the routine pre-exposure timing and reverses CDC's statement that vaccine works best before exposure. C is incorrect because HPV vaccine is preventive rather than treatment for established infection or lesions. D is incorrect because HPV causes cancers in both men and women and routine vaccination applies regardless of sex.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Explain that routine HPV vaccination begins at age 11–12 because it prevents new HPV infections before likely exposure; an immunocompetent child who starts before age 15 receives a 2-dose series 6–12 months apart, and routine vaccination applies regardless of sex.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests the current routine HPV-vaccination timing, 2-dose schedule, preventive purpose, and sex-neutral application for an immunocompetent 11-year-old, with one clearly best answer and no length or absolute-word cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. Every component is directly supported by current CDC guidance for an immunocompetent 11-year-old starting HPV vaccination.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. CDC recommends routine vaccination at age 11–12 and states that the vaccine works best before HPV exposure, not after exposure is confirmed.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. CDC explicitly states that HPV vaccination prevents new infection and does not treat existing HPV infection or disease.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. CDC states that HPV infections cause cancers in men and women, and routine adolescent HPV vaccination is not limited by sex.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone matches the current routine age, dose schedule, and preventive purpose for this immunocompetent 11-year-old; B reverses optimal timing, C reverses prevention versus treatment, and D incorrectly restricts vaccination by sex.
cueing_check: The choices are tightly balanced in length (A 168, B 175, C 169, D 166 characters), use parallel vaccination explanations, and no distractor relies on conspicuous words such as 'only' to reveal A.
